title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 10
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: A Promise Printed on Paper
passages.text:
A. A banknote is a curious object: an item of negligible material value that circulates at a stated one. Explanations of how this works usually begin with government decree, and decree is part of the answer without being the whole of it. Notes have circulated successfully where no state stood behind them, and have collapsed where one did, which indicates that the operative factor is expectation rather than authority.

B. The earliest paper money grew from deposit receipts rather than from an official design. A merchant leaving coin with a goldsmith or a temple received a written acknowledgement, and where the issuer's reliability was known, that acknowledgement could be passed to a third party instead of retrieving the coin. Nobody set out to invent currency. The receipt began to circulate because circulating it was more convenient than redeeming it, and the practice preceded any theory of what it was.

C. The step from receipt to banknote was the discovery that not everyone redeems at once. An issuer holding coin against outstanding receipts observes that only a fraction is claimed in any period, and may therefore issue receipts beyond the coin held. This is the origin of both banking's usefulness and its characteristic failure, and the two cannot be separated: an institution that lends what it holds is providing a genuine service and is simultaneously unable to meet all claims if they arrive together.

D. Confidence therefore behaves in a way that is unlike most economic quantities, because it is partly self-referential. A depositor's judgement of whether to withdraw depends on what other depositors are expected to do, and that expectation can shift on information that has no bearing on the issuer's actual position. Runs have been triggered by rumour on institutions that were solvent, and the run itself then produces the insolvency it anticipated — a sequence that is not irrational at the individual level, since a depositor who waits to verify may recover nothing.

E. Institutional responses have addressed the mechanism rather than the sentiment. Deposit insurance removes the individual incentive to be early, since a guaranteed depositor gains nothing by joining a queue, and its effect on run frequency has been substantial and measurable. It also transfers risk rather than removing it, and creates the well-documented difficulty that an insured institution faces weaker discipline from its own depositors — which is why insurance is invariably accompanied by supervision.

F. What the history suggests is that money is a social arrangement that works by being expected to work, and that this is a description rather than a criticism. The arrangement is not fragile because it is based on belief; belief in this sense is simply the aggregate of many parties acting on the reasonable assumption that others will continue to act as they have. It fails when that assumption is disturbed, and the institutions built around it are best understood as devices for making the assumption harder to disturb.

passages.title: Life Without Sunlight
passages.text:
Until the 1970s, biology textbooks stated that essentially all life depended on photosynthesis. The discovery of dense biological communities on the deep ocean floor, clustered around vents where hot mineral-laden water emerges from the crust, required that statement to be qualified rather than merely extended.

The vents are not lit and the communities around them are not sparse. Tube worms, clams and crabs occur at densities comparable to shallow reefs, in water at near-freezing temperatures kilometres below any light. The energy sustaining them comes from chemosynthesis: bacteria oxidising hydrogen sulphide and other compounds dissolved in the vent fluid, using the chemical energy released to build organic matter in the way plants use sunlight. The base of the food web is chemical rather than solar.

The relationship between the bacteria and the larger animals proved more intimate than expected. The giant tube worms characteristic of these sites have no mouth, no gut and no anus. They house symbiotic bacteria in a specialised internal organ, supply them with the raw materials collected from the water, and live on what the bacteria produce. This is not an animal feeding on microbes; it is an animal that has dispensed with feeding, and its discovery reframed how such partnerships were understood.

Vent communities are also temporary in a way that shapes their biology. Individual vents open and close over years to decades as the plumbing beneath shifts, and a community must therefore colonise new sites repeatedly across distances of hundreds of kilometres. The larvae that accomplish this drift in currents and can delay development, and populations at widely separated vents prove to be connected genetically in patterns that do not match simple geographical distance — an unresolved problem that current sampling is too sparse to settle.

The implications extended well beyond marine biology. If life can be sustained by chemical energy in darkness, the conditions considered necessary elsewhere in the solar system widen considerably, and bodies with subsurface liquid water and geological activity became candidates they had not previously been. This reasoning is legitimate and is regularly overstated: demonstrating that an environment could sustain life is not evidence that it does, and the distinction is frequently lost between the two.

Commercial interest has followed, since the mineral deposits vents produce are rich in metals for which demand is rising. Extraction proposals confront a regulatory position that is genuinely unsettled and a scientific one that is straightforward: these communities are slow to establish, dependent on a habitat that mining removes, and known from a small number of studied sites. The honest statement is not that mining would be catastrophic but that its effects cannot presently be predicted, which is a weaker claim and a harder one to act against.

passages.title: How Buildings Fail
passages.text:
Investigations into structural collapse rarely identify a single cause. What they typically find is a sequence in which several conditions, each individually tolerable, combined — and the more instructive finding is that the conditions were usually known to somebody before the event.

Design errors are the least common category and the most discussed. A structure whose calculations are wrong is normally caught, because design is checked, and the checking is one of the profession's older institutions. Failures traced to design more often involve a change made during construction whose structural consequence was not referred back — a substitution of material, a relocated opening, a connection detailed differently on site because the specified version would not fit.

Construction and maintenance account for far more. Concrete cover insufficient to protect reinforcement, bolts omitted where access was awkward, drainage that was installed and then blocked, a load-bearing wall opened during a later refurbishment by someone who did not know it was load-bearing: these are the ordinary contents of failure reports. None requires anyone to be incompetent, and most require only that information available at one moment was not available at another.

The pattern that recurs most often is a change of use. Buildings are designed for an assumed loading, and that assumption is documented at the time and rarely consulted afterwards. A floor designed for offices becomes a store room; a roof designed for snow acquires plant equipment; a hall designed for seated occupancy holds a standing crowd. Each change is reasonable to the person making it, and the cumulative demand can exceed what was intended without any single decision being unreasonable.

Warning signs are usually present and usually misread rather than ignored. Cracking, deflection and water ingress are reported, inspected and attributed to causes that are plausible and wrong — settlement, thermal movement, poor workmanship in a finish. Investigators repeatedly find that the observation was made and the interpretation was benign, which is a different failure from inattention and requires a different remedy: not more reporting, but a route by which an observation reaches someone able to recognise its significance.

The regulatory response to major failures has a consistent shape and a consistent limitation. Codes are revised, new requirements apply to new construction, and the existing stock — which is where the risk sits — is addressed only where an owner is compelled. This is why the interval after a prominent collapse shows improvement in what is being built and little change in what already stands, and why the mortality reduction attributable to codes appears slowly, over the decades in which the stock turns over rather than in the years after the rules change.
